prompt: A clinic uses a model to screen retina photos for a disease that appears in about 2% of patients. A missed case can lead to lasting vision loss. A false alarm costs one short review by a specialist. Which metric should the team put first when comparing models?
options: Recall on the disease class, since each missed patient costs far more than one extra specialist review.
Overall accuracy, since it counts every photo and so reflects both kinds of mistake in one number.
Precision on the disease class, since it keeps specialists from spending their time on healthy patients.
Specificity, since almost all photos are healthy and it measures how well those patients are cleared.
explanation:
The costs here are lopsided. Missing a sick patient can mean lasting harm, while a false alarm only costs a few minutes of a specialist's time. Recall, TP / (TP + FN), measures the share of sick patients the model catches, so it is the metric that tracks the expensive mistake.

Accuracy is dominated by the 98% of healthy photos. A model that calls everyone healthy scores 98% while catching nobody. Precision protects specialist time, which matters, but it is the cheap side of the trade in this setting. You would watch it as a constraint, not optimise it first. Specificity measures how many healthy patients are correctly cleared. It is the negative-class twin of recall and says nothing about how many sick patients were missed.
deeper: A strong answer adds a guardrail: maximise recall subject to a workload limit, such as no more than 50 referrals a day. Interviewers like hearing that you would report recall at a fixed precision or referral rate, because recall alone is easy to max out by flagging everyone.

prompt: A chat platform trains a model to flag abusive messages. About 0.1% of messages are abusive. On a large test set the model has ROC-AUC 0.97 but PR-AUC (average precision) of only 0.18. A product manager asks how both numbers can be right. Which statement correctly explains the gap?
options: The false positive rate divides by the huge pool of clean messages, so even a tiny rate can swamp the few true hits.
PR-AUC is measured only at the default 0.5 threshold, so it misses the better thresholds that ROC-AUC averages over.
ROC-AUC also credits the model for ordering clean messages correctly among themselves, which inflates it when they dominate.
PR-AUC has a random baseline of 0.5, the same as ROC-AUC, so a score of 0.18 means the model ranks worse than chance.
explanation:
ROC curves plot recall against the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN). With 999 clean messages for every abusive one, TN is enormous, so even a large number of false alarms is a small rate. Precision has no TN term, so it shows those false alarms directly.

A worked case: 1,000,000 messages, 1,000 abusive. A threshold with recall 0.80 and a false positive rate of 1% catches 800 abusive messages but also flags 9,990 clean ones. That point looks excellent on a ROC curve, yet precision is 800 / 10,790, about 0.07.

PR-AUC is threshold-free like ROC-AUC, so the option about a 0.5 threshold is wrong. ROC-AUC is the chance that a random positive outranks a random negative. Pairs of two negatives never count, so it gives no credit for ordering clean messages. The random baseline for PR-AUC is the positive rate, 0.001 here, not 0.5. So 0.18 is far better than chance, just weak in absolute terms.
deeper: In an interview, say which number matches the cost. If moderators review every flag, precision at the review budget is what matters, and PR-AUC tracks it better. A good follow-up is to report precision at a fixed recall, or recall at the number of flags the team can review each day.

prompt:
A vision model inspects 1,000 parts on a factory line. Its confusion matrix is:

- Predicted defect, actually defect: 45
- Predicted defect, actually fine: 15
- Predicted fine, actually defect: 30
- Predicted fine, actually fine: 910

What is the model's precision for the defect class? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
tp = 45
fp = 15
fn = 30
tn = 910
result = tp / (tp + fp)
explanation:
Precision asks: of the parts the model flagged as defects, how many really were? The model flagged 45 + 15 = 60 parts. Of those, 45 were real defects. So precision is 45 / 60 = 0.75.

The common mistake is to read the wrong row or column. Dividing by all real defects, 45 + 30 = 75, gives 45 / 75 = 0.60, which is recall. Another slip is to quote accuracy, (45 + 910) / 1,000 = 0.955, which looks strong only because most parts are fine. A simple habit helps: precision uses the predicted-positive counts as its denominator, recall uses the actual-positive counts.
deeper: On a factory line, precision tells you how much good stock the model sends to scrap or re-inspection, and recall tells you how many bad parts reach customers. Interviewers often follow up by asking which of the two the plant manager cares about more, and what that implies for the threshold.

prompt: A support team tests a classifier that marks tickets as urgent. On 1,000 tickets it has 30 true positives, 10 false positives and 50 false negatives. The rest are true negatives. What is the F1 score for the urgent class? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
tp = 30
fp = 10
fn = 50
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
result = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
explanation:
First get precision and recall. Precision is 30 / (30 + 10) = 0.75. Recall is 30 / (30 + 50) = 0.375. F1 is their harmonic mean: 2 × 0.75 × 0.375 / (0.75 + 0.375) = 0.5625 / 1.125 = 0.50. A shortcut gives the same result: F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) = 60 / 120 = 0.50.

The common mistake is to take the plain average, (0.75 + 0.375) / 2 ≈ 0.56. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller of the two values, so a model cannot hide weak recall behind strong precision. Notice that the true negatives play no part at all. F1 only looks at the positive class, which is why it is popular for imbalanced problems.
deeper: If missing an urgent ticket hurts more than a false alarm, F1 weights them wrongly. A strong candidate mentions F-beta, where beta above 1 leans toward recall, or simply reports recall at an agreed precision. Also remember F1 depends on the threshold you chose.

prompt: A search team scores each results page by adding up graded relevance labels, dividing each label by log₂(position + 1), and then dividing the total by the score of the best possible ordering of those same results. A perfect ranking scores 1. This metric is called ______.
explanation:
The prompt walks through the three parts of the name. Cumulative gain is the sum of relevance labels. Discounted means each label is shrunk by log₂(position + 1), so a relevant result at rank 1 counts more than the same result at rank 8. Normalized means dividing by the ideal DCG, the score you would get by sorting the results from most to least relevant. That last step puts every query on a 0 to 1 scale, so queries with many relevant results do not dominate the average.

The common mistake is to answer DCG, which has the discount but not the division by the ideal score. Others answer MRR or MAP. MRR only looks at the rank of the first relevant result, and MAP works with binary relevant or not relevant labels, so neither uses graded labels the way described here.
deeper: In practice you report NDCG@k, such as NDCG@10, because users rarely scroll further. A good interview follow-up is where the graded labels come from: human raters, or clicks and purchases, which carry position bias and need correction before you trust the metric.

prompt: A lender trained a default model after downsampling non-default loans to balance the classes. On a holdout set with the natural default rate, ROC-AUC is 0.91. Among the 1,200 holdout loans the model scored between 0.8 and 0.9, only 40% defaulted. The pricing team wants to use the scores as default probabilities. What should you conclude?
options: Ranking is strong but the scores overstate risk, so fit a calibration map on natural-rate data before pricing.
An AUC of 0.91 shows the scores are reliable probabilities, so the 40% default rate in that band is likely sampling noise.
Recalibrating will also lift AUC well above 0.91, because AUC penalises probabilities that are badly scaled.
Retrain with even heavier downsampling, so the model sees enough defaults to produce calibrated probabilities.
explanation:
Calibration means that among loans scored about 0.85, about 85% default. Here only 40% did, so the scores are far too high. AUC cannot catch this. It only checks whether defaulters are ranked above non-defaulters, and any order-preserving change to the scores leaves it the same. So a model can rank very well and still give badly wrong probabilities. The fix is to fit a calibration map, such as Platt scaling or isotonic regression, on held-out data that has the real default rate.

The noise option fails on sample size. With 1,200 loans, the standard error of a 40% rate is about 1.4 points, tiny next to a gap of at least 40 points. The option about lifting AUC is backwards: calibration keeps the ranking, so AUC stays about the same. Heavier downsampling makes things worse. Removing more non-defaults raises the default rate the model sees in training, which pushes its scores up even further.
deeper: Downsampling is a common cause of this, and there is a known prior-correction formula that maps scores back to the true base rate. Interviewers like candidates who check a reliability diagram or expected calibration error before anyone multiplies a score by a loan amount.

prompt: An online shop tests a new checkout page. Control: 12,000 users, 600 purchases. Treatment: 8,000 users, 464 purchases. Using a two-proportion z-test with a pooled proportion, what is the z statistic for treatment minus control? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
import math
n_c, x_c = 12000, 600
n_t, x_t = 8000, 464
p_c = x_c / n_c
p_t = x_t / n_t
p_pool = (x_c + x_t) / (n_c + n_t)
se = math.sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1 / n_c + 1 / n_t))
result = (p_t - p_c) / se
explanation:
Step 1, the two rates: control is 600 / 12,000 = 0.050 and treatment is 464 / 8,000 = 0.058. The difference is 0.008.

Step 2, the pooled rate, used because the null hypothesis says both groups share one rate: (600 + 464) / (12,000 + 8,000) = 1,064 / 20,000 = 0.0532.

Step 3, the standard error: √(0.0532 × 0.9468 × (1/12,000 + 1/8,000)) = √(0.05037 × 0.00020833) ≈ 0.003239.

Step 4, z = 0.008 / 0.003239 ≈ 2.47. That is above 1.96, so the lift is significant at the 5% level for a two-sided test.

The common mistake is the standard error. If you use only one group size, √(p(1 − p) / 12,000), you get about 3.90, which badly overstates the evidence. Using separate, unpooled variances gives about 2.44. That is close here, but the pooled form is the standard one for testing whether the two rates are equal.
deeper: A significant z does not end the conversation. Interviewers ask whether the test ran for its planned length, whether anyone peeked and stopped early, and whether the sample split matched the planned ratio. A split that differs from plan, called sample ratio mismatch, often signals a bug in assignment.

subtopic: choosing a threshold from business costs
prompt: A telecom company has a churn model that outputs a probability for each customer. The retention team can make at most 300 calls a week. Each call costs $15. A churner who gets a call stays 25% of the time, and a customer who stays is worth $400. Calling a customer who was not going to churn gains nothing. How would you choose the score threshold for who gets a call?
answer: I would set the threshold from expected value, not from 0.5. A call to a customer with churn probability p is worth p × 0.25 × $400 = $100p and costs $15, so it pays off when p is above 0.15. That is the break-even threshold. Capacity also binds. If more than 300 customers score above 0.15, I would call the 300 highest scores, so the real threshold becomes the 300th score. If fewer clear 0.15, I would call only those and leave spare capacity unused. This only works if the probabilities are calibrated, so I would check a reliability plot first. Then I would confirm the value with a holdout group that gets no calls, and revisit the threshold when costs, save rates or the score distribution change.
points: Compare the cost of a wasted call with the value lost from a missed churner
Break-even probability is cost divided by value times save rate, here 0.15
The 300-call cap means taking the top 300 scores when many clear break-even
Scores must be calibrated for the break-even rule to hold
Validate with a no-call holdout and update the threshold as inputs change
explanation:
The threshold is a business decision, so it should come from what each mistake costs. A false positive wastes a $15 call. A missed churner who could have been saved loses the expected value of the call, which is 0.25 × $400 = $100 for a sure churner. Setting p × 100 = 15 gives p = 0.15. Above that, a call is worth more than it costs on average.

The common mistake is to keep the default 0.5 or to pick the threshold that maximises F1. Both ignore the costs. Here 0.5 would skip many customers who are worth calling. The second mistake is to forget the capacity cap. When demand exceeds 300 calls, you rank by score and stop at 300, and the cap, not the break-even point, sets the cut. Finally, the break-even rule assumes a score of 0.2 really means a 20% chance of churn. An uncalibrated model breaks that link.
deeper: A strong candidate notes that the 25% save rate is not the same for everyone. Some customers would stay anyway and some cannot be saved. Uplift modelling targets the customers whose behaviour the call actually changes, which often beats ranking by churn risk alone.

prompt: A logistics company predicts which conveyor motors will fail within the next 24 hours. In the test data, 99.0% of motor-days have no failure. The new model scores 99.2% accuracy, and a manager asks what that number tells them. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Very little about failures, since always predicting "no failure" scores 99.0% too.
That the model correctly catches about 99% of the motors that are about to fail.
That about 0.8% of the motors the model flags will turn out to be false alarms.
That the model is reliable, since 99.2% on a large test set cannot happen by luck.
explanation:
Accuracy counts every correct prediction, and here almost every motor-day is a non-failure. A model that always says "no failure" is right 99.0% of the time while catching nothing. The new model beats that baseline by only 0.2 points, and that small gap fits very different behaviours. With 0.8% of motor-days wrong and 1.0% being failures, the model could catch every failure while raising a few false alarms, or catch only one failure in five and never raise an alarm. Accuracy alone cannot tell these apart.

The option about catching 99% of failing motors confuses accuracy with recall, which looks only at real failures. The option about 0.8% false alarms confuses the overall error rate with the share of flags that are wrong, which is 1 minus precision. A large test set makes the 99.2% estimate precise, but a precise estimate of an uninformative number is still uninformative.
deeper: In an interview, name the majority-class baseline first, then ask for the confusion matrix. For maintenance, recall on failures and the number of false alarms per week are what the operations team feels. A cost per missed failure and per needless inspection turns those into one number a manager can act on.

prompt:
An airport tests a model that flags checked bags for a manual search. On 5,000 test bags the results are:

- Flagged, bag held a banned item: 36
- Not flagged, bag held a banned item: 4
- Flagged, bag was clean: 248
- Not flagged, bag was clean: 4,712

What is the model's specificity? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
tp = 36
fn = 4
fp = 248
tn = 4712
result = tn / (tn + fp)
explanation:
Specificity is the share of truly negative cases that the model correctly leaves alone: TN / (TN + FP). Here the negatives are the clean bags. There are 4,712 + 248 = 4,960 of them, and the model left 4,712 unflagged. So specificity is 4,712 / 4,960 = 0.95.

Recall is the same idea for the positive class: TP / (TP + FN) = 36 / (36 + 4) = 0.90. Together the two describe how the model treats each true class on its own.

The most common mistake is to divide by all 5,000 bags, which gives 4,712 / 5,000 ≈ 0.94. That puts the bags with banned items into the denominator, even though specificity is only about clean bags. Another slip is to use the flagged column, 36 / (36 + 248) ≈ 0.13, which is precision. Notice how that low precision sits beside a high specificity. With so many clean bags, even 5% of them flagged swamps the 36 real hits.
deeper: Recall and specificity each look inside one true class, so they stay the same if banned items become rarer or more common, as long as the model behaves the same on each kind of bag. Precision does not. That is why screening teams quote recall and specificity for the test itself, then work out flag volume for the traffic they really see.

prompt: A forum's moderation model reviewed 20,000 harmless posts and wrongly removed 300 of them. The figure 300 / 20,000 = 0.015, which is FP / (FP + TN), is the model's ______. It is also the horizontal axis of a ROC curve.
explanation:
The false positive rate looks only at the true negatives, here the harmless posts, and asks what share of them the model wrongly flagged. Its denominator is every actual negative: the ones wrongly removed (FP) plus the ones correctly left up (TN). So 300 / 20,000 = 1.5%.

The usual mix-up is with the false discovery rate, FP / (FP + TP), which is 1 minus precision. That one divides by everything the model removed and asks how many removals were mistakes. The two can be very different. If the model also removed 700 truly harmful posts, the false discovery rate would be 300 / 1,000 = 30% while the false positive rate stays at 1.5%. Another slip is to call it the false negative rate, which is about harmful posts the model missed. The false positive rate equals 1 minus specificity, so that form is accepted too.
deeper: On a ROC curve each threshold gives one point, with the false positive rate on the x-axis and recall on the y-axis. In moderation, a rate that sounds tiny can still mean thousands of wrongly removed posts a day at scale, so teams often turn the rate into an expected count of appeals.

prompt: A B2B sales team scores leads with a model and sends every lead scoring above 0.4 to a sales rep. Reps complain that too many leads are poor, so the team raises the threshold to 0.7. Nothing else changes. What usually happens to precision and recall for the "good lead" class?
options: Recall falls or stays the same, and precision usually rises.
Recall usually rises, and precision falls or stays the same.
Both usually rise, since only the most confident leads are sent.
Neither changes, since the threshold does not alter the scores.
explanation:
Raising the threshold means fewer leads get labelled good. Every lead above 0.7 was already above 0.4, so the new set of flagged leads is a subset of the old one. The model can only lose true positives, never gain them, so recall (true positives divided by all truly good leads) falls or stays the same. The leads dropped are the ones scored between 0.4 and 0.7, which are usually weaker, so the share of flagged leads that are good, precision, usually goes up. It is not guaranteed. If that dropped band happened to be rich in good leads, precision could dip.

The option claiming recall rises while precision falls has both directions backwards. Sending fewer leads cannot find more good ones, and it trims the weakest leads first. Both rising is the hope behind the change, but it ignores the good leads scored between 0.4 and 0.7 that are now missed. The scores do stay the same, but precision and recall are computed from the yes or no decisions, and those change.
deeper: A strong answer adds that the right threshold comes from rep capacity and the value of a won deal, not from a round number. Plotting precision and recall against the threshold shows the team exactly how many good leads the move from 0.4 to 0.7 gives up.

prompt: A hospital builds a model that predicts which patients will miss their next appointment. On a held-out set it has ROC-AUC 0.82, and the default threshold is 0.5. Which statement about the 0.82 is correct?
options: Pick a patient who missed and one who attended at random, and the model scores the no-show higher 82% of the time.
At the 0.5 threshold, the model labels 82% of all patients correctly as either a no-show or an attendee.
Of the patients the model flags as likely no-shows at the 0.5 threshold, 82% really do miss their appointment.
Moving the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 would change the 0.82, because more patients would then be flagged as no-shows.
explanation:
ROC-AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, with ties counted as half. Here the positives are patients who missed. So 0.82 says the model orders a random missed-attended pair correctly 82% of the time. It is a statement about ranking, built from every possible threshold at once.

That is why the option about moving the threshold to 0.3 is wrong. A new threshold picks a different point on the same ROC curve but leaves the area under it untouched. The option about labelling 82% of patients correctly describes accuracy at 0.5, which needs a cut-off and depends heavily on how common no-shows are. The option about 82% of flagged patients describes precision at 0.5, also a single-threshold number. A model with ROC-AUC 0.82 can have precision far below or above 82%, depending on the threshold and the no-show rate.
deeper: Interviewers like the pairwise reading because it shows why AUC ignores calibration. Any change that keeps the order of scores, such as squaring them, leaves AUC the same. A good follow-up is that AUC helps compare models, but the clinic still needs a threshold chosen from how many reminder calls staff can make.

prompt: A legal team tests a model that scores emails for attorney-client privilege. On a tiny check set, the three privileged emails score 0.92, 0.70 and 0.45. The four non-privileged emails score 0.80, 0.45, 0.30 and 0.10. Compute ROC-AUC by comparing every privileged email with every non-privileged one, counting a tie as half a correct pair. Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
explanation:
ROC-AUC equals the share of positive-negative pairs that the model orders correctly. With 3 privileged and 4 non-privileged emails there are 3 × 4 = 12 pairs.

- 0.92 beats all four negatives: 4 pairs.
- 0.70 loses to 0.80 but beats 0.45, 0.30 and 0.10: 3 pairs.
- 0.45 loses to 0.80, ties with 0.45 and beats 0.30 and 0.10: 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 pairs.

The total is 4 + 3 + 2.5 = 9.5 correct pairs, and 9.5 / 12 ≈ 0.79.

The most common slip is the tie. Dropping it gives 9 / 12 = 0.75, and counting it as a full win gives 10 / 12 ≈ 0.83. Counting a tie as half matches the area under the ROC curve, where a tied score moves the curve diagonally. Another mistake is to compare only neighbouring scores in the sorted list instead of every positive with every negative.
deeper: This pair-counting view is the Mann-Whitney U statistic divided by the number of pairs. Nobody counts by hand in practice, but interviewers use small cases like this to check you know what AUC measures. It also explains why AUC is unchanged by any order-preserving change to the scores.

prompt: A bank's model flags payments that may be going to the wrong account. Missing one is far worse than an extra manual check, so the team stops using F1. They switch to a harmonic-mean metric in which recall counts β times as much as precision, and they pick β = 2. The general name for this weighted metric is the ______.
explanation:
The F-beta score is (1 + β²) × P × R / (β² × P + R), a weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall. With β = 1 it is the ordinary F1, which treats the two equally. With β = 2 recall gets more weight, so a model that misses fewer wrong-account payments scores better even if it raises more checks. For example, with precision 0.5 and recall 0.9, F1 ≈ 0.64 but F2 ≈ 0.78. With β below 1, such as 0.5, precision gets the extra weight instead.

A common mistake is to think a weighted arithmetic mean, such as 0.2 × P + 0.8 × R, does the same job. An arithmetic mean lets a model hide a terrible precision behind a high recall. A model that flags every payment has recall 1 and still scores at least 0.8 that way. The harmonic mean stays low whenever either part is very low, which is why the F family uses it. Another slip is to think a larger β favours precision. It favours recall.
deeper: In interviews, say why you chose β, not just its value. A strong answer ties it to costs, for example a misdirected payment costing far more than a five-minute manual review. Many teams still report precision and recall next to F2, because one blended number hides which side moved.

prompt:
A support-ticket router sorts 1,000 tickets into three classes. For each class, here is how many tickets it predicted and how many of those predictions were right:

- Billing: predicted 600, correct 540
- Technical: predicted 350, correct 315
- Legal: predicted 50, correct 15

Each ticket gets exactly one predicted class. What is micro-averaged precision minus macro-averaged precision? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
pred = [600, 350, 50]
correct = [540, 315, 15]
macro = sum(c / p for c, p in zip(correct, pred)) / len(pred)
micro = sum(correct) / sum(pred)
result = micro - macro
explanation:
Macro averaging computes precision for each class, then takes the plain mean. Billing is 540 / 600 = 0.90, technical is 315 / 350 = 0.90 and legal is 15 / 50 = 0.30. The macro average is (0.90 + 0.90 + 0.30) / 3 = 0.70.

Micro averaging pools the counts first: (540 + 315 + 15) / (600 + 350 + 50) = 870 / 1,000 = 0.87. Since every ticket gets exactly one label, micro precision here equals plain accuracy.

The gap is 0.87 − 0.70 = 0.17. Micro weights each class by how often it is predicted, so the 50 legal predictions barely move it. Macro gives legal a full third of the vote, so its weak 0.30 drags the average down.

The common mistake is to weight each class precision by how many tickets that class predicted and call the result macro. (0.90 × 600 + 0.90 × 350 + 0.30 × 50) / 1,000 = 0.87, which is the micro figure again, and the gap wrongly disappears.
deeper: Which average to report depends on what matters. If legal tickets carry the most risk, macro or a per-class table keeps their poor precision visible, while micro hides it behind the big classes. Scikit-learn also offers a weighted average, which weights each class by its number of true tickets.

prompt:
A courier's model predicts the chance that each parcel arrives late. Four parcels come back:

- Late, predicted 0.9
- On time, predicted 0.2
- Late, predicted 0.8
- On time, predicted 0.99

The numbers are the predicted probability of being late. Using the natural log, what is the mean log loss over the four parcels? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
import math
y = [1, 0, 1, 0]
p = [0.9, 0.2, 0.8, 0.99]
losses = [-(t * math.log(q) + (1 - t) * math.log(1 - q)) for t, q in zip(y, p)]
result = sum(losses) / len(losses)
explanation:
Log loss charges −ln of the probability the model gave to what really happened. For a late parcel that is −ln(p), and for an on-time parcel it is −ln(1 − p).

- Late at 0.9: −ln(0.9) ≈ 0.105
- On time at 0.2: −ln(0.8) ≈ 0.223
- Late at 0.8: −ln(0.8) ≈ 0.223
- On time at 0.99: −ln(0.01) ≈ 4.605

The sum is about 5.157, and the mean is 5.157 / 4 ≈ 1.29.

The last parcel does almost all the damage. The model was 99% sure it would be late, and it was not. Without it, the mean of the other three is only about 0.18. Log loss grows without limit as the probability given to the true outcome nears zero.

The common mistake is to use −ln(p) for every row, including the on-time parcels. That gives about 0.49, because it charges the confident wrong prediction almost nothing and charges the good 0.2 prediction heavily.
deeper: This is why libraries clip probabilities away from exactly 0 and 1, and why one mislabelled row can wreck a leaderboard score. In an interview, mention that log loss judges calibration as well as ranking, so two models with the same AUC can have very different log loss.

prompt: A power utility forecasts hourly electricity demand. Small misses are cheap to cover, but a large miss forces it to buy emergency power at many times the normal price. Which error metric best reflects that cost when comparing forecasting models?
options: RMSE, because squaring each error makes a few large misses count far more than many small ones.
MAE, because it is in megawatts like the forecast, while RMSE is in megawatts squared.
MAE, because it is always at least as large as RMSE, so it gives the more cautious figure for planning.
MAPE, because percentage errors are largest at peak hours when demand is highest.
explanation:
RMSE squares each error before averaging, then takes a square root. Squaring makes one 100 MW miss count as much as a hundred 10 MW misses, so a model that sometimes misses badly scores poorly even if it is usually close. That matches a cost that grows sharply with the size of the miss.

The option about units is wrong because the square root brings RMSE back to megawatts, the same units as MAE. The option about MAE being larger has it backwards. RMSE is always greater than or equal to MAE, and the two are equal only when every error has the same size. The MAPE option fails because actual demand sits in the denominator. At peak hours that denominator is largest, so the same megawatt miss becomes a smaller percentage, the opposite of what the utility needs.

RMSE is still symmetric, so it treats over- and under-forecasts alike. If only one direction is costly, an asymmetric loss such as quantile loss fits even better.
deeper: A strong answer reports both. MAE gives planners a typical miss in plain megawatts, and the gap between RMSE and MAE shows how much the large misses matter. Interviewers may also ask how you would train for this cost, which leads to quantile or other asymmetric losses.

prompt: A bakery forecasts daily loaves for one shop. Over five days the errors (forecast minus actual) are +2, −4, +1, −3 and +10 loaves. The team already reports an MAE of 4.0 loaves. What is the RMSE? Give it in loaves to 1 decimal place.
check:
import math
errors = [2, -4, 1, -3, 10]
result = math.sqrt(sum(e * e for e in errors) / len(errors))
explanation:
RMSE squares each error, averages the squares, then takes the square root. The squares are 4, 16, 1, 9 and 100. Their sum is 130, the mean is 130 / 5 = 26, and √26 ≈ 5.1 loaves.

For comparison, MAE averages the sizes of the errors: (2 + 4 + 1 + 3 + 10) / 5 = 20 / 5 = 4.0. RMSE is higher because the one 10-loaf miss supplies 100 of the 130 in the squared sum. If all five errors had been 4 loaves, RMSE and MAE would both be 4.0.

The common mistakes skip or reorder a step. Averaging the signed errors gives (2 − 4 + 1 − 3 + 10) / 5 = 1.2, which is the bias, not the size of the error, because positive and negative misses cancel. Taking the square root of the sum instead of the mean gives √130 ≈ 11.4. Forgetting the square root leaves 26, which is the MSE in loaves squared.
deeper: The ratio RMSE / MAE is a quick outlier check. Here it is about 1.27, which hints that one day drove most of the error. In a forecasting review, a strong candidate would look at that day, perhaps a holiday or a local event, before tuning the model.

prompt: A team predicts house sale prices. On the training data R² is 0.91. On a held-out test set from a later year, scikit-learn's `r2_score` returns −0.15. What does the negative test score mean?
options: The model's test predictions have more squared error than predicting the test set's mean price for every house.
R² cannot be below zero, so the test score points to a bug in how the metric was computed on the test set.
The model explains 15% of the price variance on the test set, but with predictions that run the wrong way.
The model needs more features, since adding features always raises R² on any data set, test sets included.
explanation:
R² is 1 − SS_res / SS_tot. SS_res is the squared error of the model's predictions, and SS_tot is the squared error of always predicting the mean of the actual values. A score below zero means SS_res is larger than SS_tot, so the model does worse than that constant guess. With a training R² of 0.91, the likely causes are overfitting or a shift in prices between the years.

The belief that R² cannot be negative comes from least squares fits with an intercept, scored on their own training data, where the fit can always fall back to the mean. On new data there is no such floor. Reading −0.15 as 15% explained the wrong way is not how R² works. It is simply a worse-than-baseline score. Adding features never lowers training R² for least squares, but on a test set extra features often make things worse by adding variance.
deeper: Interviewers like to follow up with adjusted R², which penalises extra features, and with why a later-year test set is the honest one. If prices rose overall, the model may be biased low across the board. Plotting residuals against time or predicted price usually shows this quickly.

prompt: A grocery chain scores its daily demand forecasts with MAPE across 5,000 products. Many products sell only 1 to 3 units a day, and days with zero sales are left out of the metric. The weekly MAPE reads 340% and jumps around even when the forecasts barely change. What is the best diagnosis and fix?
options: Small actuals in the denominator turn tiny misses into huge percentages. Report WAPE, total absolute error over total sales.
MAPE treats over- and under-forecasts the same, which hides forecast bias. Report RMSE, which separates the two kinds of miss.
Products sell on very different scales, which MAPE cannot handle. Report RMSE pooled across all 5,000 products and days instead.
The slow sellers are just noise. Keep MAPE but drop products that sell under 3 units a day from the report.
explanation:
MAPE averages |actual − forecast| / actual. When the actual is 1 unit, forecasting 3 is a 200% error, and a product that sells 1 unit one day and 3 the next swings between 200% and 0% with the same forecast. Slow sellers like this push the average to 340%. WAPE sums the absolute errors over all products and days and divides by total sales once, so a 2-unit miss counts as 2 units, not 200%.

The option about symmetry is wrong twice. MAPE is not symmetric: an under-forecast costs at most 100%, while an over-forecast has no cap, so MAPE quietly rewards forecasting low. RMSE squares away the sign, so it does not separate the two kinds of miss either. Pooled RMSE does not fix scale. It is in units, so high-volume products dominate it, and MAPE was scale-free to begin with. Dropping slow sellers hides products whose stock still has to be planned, rather than fixing the metric.
deeper: Other common choices are MASE, which scales errors by the error of a naive forecast, and reporting error per product family. In an interview, add that you would track bias separately, as the sum of signed errors over total sales, because neither WAPE nor RMSE shows whether forecasts run high or low.

prompt: A recipe app shows a user a ranked list of 10 recommended recipes. Using the recipes the user later saved as ground truth, 6 recipes in the whole catalogue are relevant to them. In the ranked list, relevant recipes sit at positions 1, 3, 4, 7 and 9. What is recall@5? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
relevant_positions = [1, 3, 4, 7, 9]
total_relevant = 6
k = 5
hits = sum(1 for p in relevant_positions if p <= k)
result = hits / total_relevant
explanation:
Recall@k asks what share of all relevant items appear in the top k. The top 5 positions hold relevant recipes at positions 1, 3 and 4, so there are 3 hits. There are 6 relevant recipes in the whole catalogue, so recall@5 = 3 / 6 = 0.50.

The common mistake is dividing by k. That gives 3 / 5 = 0.60, which is precision@5, the share of the shown slots that are relevant. Another slip is to count the hits at positions 7 and 9, which sit outside the top 5. A third is to divide by the 5 relevant recipes that appear somewhere in the list instead of all 6 in the catalogue. The sixth relevant recipe was never shown, and recall@k is meant to charge the model for that. Also note that recall@5 can never exceed 5 divided by the number of relevant items, so with many relevant items even a perfect list scores low.
deeper: Precision@k fits a fixed set of slots, such as a carousel of five recipes, where every slot should be useful. Recall@k fits a retrieval stage that hands candidates to a re-ranker, where an item missed early can never be shown. A strong candidate also asks where the ground truth came from, since saves miss recipes the user never saw.

prompt:
A help-centre search is tested on five queries. Each query has one or more relevant articles, found at these ranks:

- Query 1: rank 1
- Query 2: ranks 3 and 5
- Query 3: no relevant article in the top 10
- Query 4: ranks 2 and 4
- Query 5: rank 4

A query with no relevant article in the top 10 scores 0. What is the mean reciprocal rank? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
first_relevant = [1, 3, None, 2, 4]
rr = [0.0 if r is None else 1.0 / r for r in first_relevant]
result = sum(rr) / len(rr)
explanation:
Reciprocal rank uses only the first relevant result for each query and scores it as 1 divided by its rank. The later relevant results for queries 2 and 4 do not count.

- Query 1: 1 / 1 = 1.000
- Query 2: 1 / 3 ≈ 0.333
- Query 3: 0
- Query 4: 1 / 2 = 0.500
- Query 5: 1 / 4 = 0.250

The sum is about 2.083, and the mean over 5 queries is about 0.42.

One common mistake is to drop query 3 and average over four queries. That gives about 0.52 and hides the query that failed completely. Another is to average the first ranks and then invert, turning ranks 1, 3, 2 and 4 into a mean rank of 2.5 and a score of 0.40. That is not the same calculation, and a single deep result can swing it a lot. A third slip is to add 1/5 and 1/4 for the extra relevant articles in queries 2 and 4.
deeper: MRR suits tasks where the user wants one answer, such as a help article or a known product page. It ignores every relevant result after the first, so it fits poorly when users read several results. For the retriever in an LLM app, teams often report MRR next to recall@k.

prompt:
A hotel search returns five results for a query. Raters labelled each one from 0 (useless) to 3 (perfect). In the order shown, the labels are 2, 3, 0, 1, 3.

Use DCG@3 = Σ relᵢ / log₂(i + 1) over positions i = 1 to 3, with the label itself as the gain. IDCG@3 is the DCG@3 of the best possible ordering of all five results. What is NDCG@3? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
explanation:
First the DCG of the list as shown. The discounts for positions 1, 2 and 3 are log₂(2) = 1, log₂(3) ≈ 1.585 and log₂(4) = 2.

DCG@3 = 2 / 1 + 3 / 1.585 + 0 / 2 ≈ 2 + 1.893 + 0 = 3.893.

Next the ideal. Sorting all five labels gives 3, 3, 2, 1, 0, so the best possible top three is 3, 3, 2.

IDCG@3 = 3 / 1 + 3 / 1.585 + 2 / 2 ≈ 3 + 1.893 + 1 = 5.893.

NDCG@3 = 3.893 / 5.893 ≈ 0.66.

The common mistake is to build the ideal only from the three results that were shown in the top 3. Sorting 2, 3, 0 gives an ideal DCG of 3 + 2 / 1.585 ≈ 4.262 and an NDCG of about 0.91. That flatters the ranker, because it is never charged for leaving a perfect hotel down at position 5. Another slip is to use log₂(i) as the discount, which divides by zero at position 1.
deeper: Many teams use the gain 2^rel − 1 instead of the raw label, which rewards perfect results much more than good ones. The two choices give different numbers, so always state which one you used. NDCG is then averaged over many queries, and queries with no relevant results need a rule, since their IDCG is 0.

prompt: An internal company directory lets staff type a colleague's name and see a ranked list of profiles. Each query has exactly one correct profile, and people read from the top and stop at the first match. Which offline metric fits this search best?
options: MRR, since it scores each query by how high its one correct profile sits in the list.
Precision@10, since it counts how many of the top 10 results are the right person for each query.
NDCG@10, since it rewards graded relevance across the whole first page of results.
Recall@10, since what matters most is that the right profile appears somewhere on the first page.
explanation:
With one correct answer per query and users who stop at the first match, what matters is the rank of that one profile. Reciprocal rank scores rank 1 as 1, rank 2 as 0.5 and rank 3 as about 0.33, and MRR averages this over queries. It tracks how far down people must read.

Precision@10 fits a different job. With one correct profile, its best possible score is 1 / 10 = 0.1, and it gives the same score whether the profile is at rank 1 or rank 10. Recall@10 has the same blind spot, since it only asks whether the profile made the first page. NDCG@10 is built for graded relevance spread across many results, and this directory has neither: one profile is right and the rest are simply wrong. With a single relevant item NDCG still rewards higher placement, but its gentle log discount scores rank 3 at 0.5, which suits a user who keeps scanning, not one who stops at the first match.
deeper: If the team also cares how often the right person is the very first result, it can report success@1 next to MRR. For a product search where raters grade results as perfect, good or fair, NDCG becomes the better choice, and precision@k fits a feed with a fixed number of slots.

prompt: A hospital team checks the calibration of a readmission model. They sort 20,000 test patients into 10 equal-width bins by predicted probability and plot a reliability diagram: mean predicted probability on the x-axis and the observed readmission rate on the y-axis. They also report expected calibration error (ECE). Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A bin plotted below the diagonal is one where the model predicted more readmissions than actually happened.
ECE weights each bin's gap by its share of patients, so a large gap in a nearly empty bin adds very little.
A model that gives every patient the overall readmission rate can have ECE near 0 while ranking no one usefully.
A bin plotted above the diagonal is one where the model's scores are too high and should be pulled down.
ECE comes out the same whatever number of bins you choose, so the bin count does not need reporting.
If recalibration lowers ECE, the model's ROC-AUC must have gone up by a similar amount as well.
explanation:
A point below the diagonal has an x value (what the model predicted) higher than its y value (what happened). If patients in a bin were scored 0.40 on average but only 25% were readmitted, the model overestimates risk there, and its scores for that bin should be pulled down. ECE is the weighted average of the gaps |observed − predicted| across bins, with each bin weighted by the share of patients in it, so a 30-point gap in a bin with 15 patients barely moves it. And calibration is not discrimination. A model that predicts the base rate for everyone is perfectly calibrated on average but cannot separate high-risk from low-risk patients.

The option about points above the diagonal has it backwards. There the observed rate is higher than predicted, so the scores are too low. ECE does depend on the binning: more bins means fewer patients per bin and noisier gaps, which tends to push ECE up, so the bin count should be reported. Finally, a monotonic recalibration such as Platt scaling keeps the order of the scores, so ROC-AUC stays the same while ECE falls.
deeper: In an interview, pair ECE with the diagram itself and a count per bin. A single ECE number hides where the miscalibration sits, and for a readmission model the high-risk bins usually drive care decisions. A strong candidate also mentions equal-count bins, which avoid near-empty bins at the extremes.

prompt: A support vector machine flags toxic product reviews. Its raw outputs are margin scores, not probabilities. The team holds out a calibration set, fits a logistic regression that takes the raw score as its only input and the true label as the target, and then reports that regression's output as the probability of toxicity. This recalibration method is called ______.
explanation:
Platt scaling fits p = 1 / (1 + exp(−(a·s + b))), where s is the raw score and a and b are learned on held-out data. That is exactly a one-feature logistic regression on the score. Because the sigmoid is monotonic, the order of the reviews does not change, so ranking metrics such as ROC-AUC stay the same while the probabilities become usable.

The most common wrong answer is isotonic regression. It also recalibrates, but it fits a free-form, step-shaped increasing function instead of a sigmoid. It needs more calibration data and can overfit when the set is small. Some people answer temperature scaling, which divides a neural network's logits by one learned number and has no separate shift term. It is a close cousin, but the method described here, with a slope and an intercept on the score, is Platt scaling. Fitting the map on the training data instead of a held-out set is the other classic slip, because the model has already fitted those examples, so their scores are more extreme than scores on new reviews.
deeper: A good follow-up is when to pick each method. Platt scaling suits small calibration sets and S-shaped distortion, which is typical of SVMs and boosted trees. Isotonic regression handles odd shapes but wants thousands of examples. Either way, check a reliability diagram before and after.

prompt: A model flags faulty sensor readings on a wind farm. In the test set, 5% of readings are faulty. The model scores a PR-AUC (average precision) of 0.30, and a teammate says that is worse than a coin flip. What PR-AUC would a model with random scores get on this test set, in expectation?
options: About 0.05, the share of faulty readings, so 0.30 is about six times the random level.
About 0.50, the same as the random ROC-AUC, so 0.30 means the model ranks worse than chance.
About 0.00, because random scores almost never put a faulty reading at the top of the list.
About 0.95, the share of normal readings, because random scores get most of those right.
explanation:
With random scores, the readings above any threshold are a random sample of the test set, so about 5% of them are faulty at every threshold. Precision stays near 0.05 all the way along the recall axis, and the area under that flat line is about 0.05. So the baseline for PR-AUC is the positive rate, and 0.30 is a real gain over it.

The option claiming 0.50 mixes up the two curves. ROC-AUC has a random baseline of 0.5 whatever the class mix, but PR-AUC does not. The option claiming 0.00 forgets that precision is a share, not a count. Random scores still put some faulty readings near the top, about 5% of whatever is flagged. The option claiming 0.95 uses the wrong class. Precision and recall here are about the faulty class, so the normal readings do not set the baseline.
deeper: Always say the positive rate next to a PR-AUC. A score of 0.30 is strong when positives are 1% and weak when they are 25%. It also means PR-AUC values from test sets with different class mixes cannot be compared directly.

prompt:
A travel site wants to test a new booking flow. The current booking rate is 4.0%, and the smallest lift worth detecting is a 10% relative increase. The test uses a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 80% power, so use 1.96 for the significance level and 0.84 for power. Use the standard per-arm sample size formula with unpooled variances:

n = (1.96 + 0.84)² × (p₁(1 − p₁) + p₂(1 − p₂)) / (p₂ − p₁)²

Round n up to a whole user. The site gets 6,000 new eligible users a day, split evenly between control and treatment. How many whole days must the test run to reach the required sample in both arms? Give a whole number.
check:
import math
p1 = 0.04
p2 = p1 * 1.10
z = 1.96 + 0.84
n = math.ceil(z ** 2 * (p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2)) / (p2 - p1) ** 2)
per_arm_per_day = 6000 / 2
result = math.ceil(n / per_arm_per_day)
explanation:
Step 1, turn the relative lift into rates: p₁ = 0.040 and p₂ = 0.040 × 1.10 = 0.044, so p₂ − p₁ = 0.004.

Step 2, the variance term: 0.04 × 0.96 + 0.044 × 0.956 = 0.0384 + 0.042064 = 0.080464.

Step 3, n = 2.8² × 0.080464 / 0.004² = 7.84 × 0.080464 / 0.000016 ≈ 39,427.4, which rounds up to 39,428 users per arm.

Step 4, each arm gets 6,000 / 2 = 3,000 users a day, so 39,428 / 3,000 ≈ 13.14 days. You cannot stop part way through a day and still have enough users, so the test needs 14 days.

The most common mistake is in step 4: dividing one arm's sample by the full 6,000 a day gives about 7 days, half of what is needed. The second is using the relative lift, 0.10, as p₂ − p₁. That makes n tiny and the test hopelessly underpowered. Small absolute gaps on a low base rate are what make sample sizes large.
deeper: Here 14 days is also two full weeks, which is good, because weekday and weekend users often behave differently. Interviewers like to hear that you would round up to whole weeks anyway, and that halving the detectable lift roughly quadruples the sample needed.

prompt: A growth team plans a four-week A/B test of a new onboarding email. The analyst computes the p-value for sign-up rate every morning and plans to stop and ship the first day it drops below 0.05. Which statement best describes the problem and a sound fix?
options: Each daily look is another chance to cross 0.05 by luck, so false positives run well above 5%. Fix the sample size up front or use a sequential test built for repeated looks.
Daily looks are fine because each p-value uses all the data collected so far, so a value below 0.05 on any day is valid. The only fix needed is to log the day the test stopped.
Stopping early mainly causes false negatives, because the test ends with less data than planned. The fix is to keep looking daily but always run at least one week past the planned end.
The extra risk from daily looks is small, and switching to a one-sided test halves the false positive rate, which more than offsets it. The fix is to use a one-sided test from the start.
explanation:
A p-value below 0.05 means a 5% false positive rate only for a single test done once at a planned sample size. Under the null hypothesis the p-value drifts up and down as data arrives. Stopping the first time it dips below 0.05 gives luck many chances to win. A simulation of a test with no real effect puts the false positive rate near 25% with 20 looks and near 27% with the 28 daily looks of a four-week test, more than five times the planned rate. The fixes are to fix the sample size and analyse once, or to use a method designed for repeated looks, such as a group sequential design with alpha spending or always-valid p-values.

The option saying daily looks are fine misses that each extra look is another test, so using all the data does not help. The option about false negatives has the main harm the wrong way round. This stopping rule only stops on a significant result, so it inflates false positives. The one-sided option is wrong too: a one-sided test at 0.05 still has a 5% false positive rate for a single look, and peeking inflates it just the same.
deeper: Teams often want to stop early for good reasons, such as a harmful change. A strong answer separates the two: guardrail checks that may stop a test for harm, and a pre-planned decision rule for success. Mention alpha spending or sequential testing by name, then explain the idea in one sentence.

prompt: A food delivery app runs a two-week A/B test of a new restaurant ranking on its home feed. Users are split 50/50 at random, and both arms order from the same restaurants and use the same couriers. Which of these are real threats to trusting the result? Select all that apply.
options: Treatment users pile onto a few top-ranked restaurants, which slows those kitchens for control users as well.
Of 2,000,000 assigned users, the logs show 1,016,000 in treatment and 984,000 in control.
Regular users click more in the first days because the feed looks new, and the gap shrinks in week two.
The team tracked 25 metrics and the write-up highlights the 2 that reached p < 0.05.
The two arms differ slightly in average user age, by about what random assignment would produce.
The test ran two full weeks instead of a few days, so it covers every day of the week twice.
explanation:
Four of these break the test. Shared kitchens mean the arms interfere with each other: treatment can make control look worse, so the measured gap overstates the true effect. The split is 50.8% to 49.2%. That sounds small, but with 2 million users chance alone rarely moves it by more than 0.1 points, and a chi-square test gives about 512, so the gap is far too large to be luck. This sample ratio mismatch points to a bug in assignment or logging. The early burst that fades is a novelty effect, so the first-week lift will not last. And with 25 metrics at 0.05, you expect about one false hit by chance, so two highlighted wins are weak evidence without a correction.

The small age difference is not a threat. Random assignment balances groups only on average, and small chance differences are exactly what the p-value already accounts for. Running two full weeks is a strength, because it averages over weekday and weekend behaviour instead of capturing only part of the cycle.
deeper: Marketplaces are where interference bites hardest. Interviewers like candidates who suggest switchback tests (alternating the whole market between arms by time slot) or splitting by city. Checking sample ratio mismatch before reading any metric is a habit worth naming.

prompt: A job board trains a new search ranker on click logs from its current ranker. On a held-out week of those logs, the new model predicts clicks better, with AUC 0.74 against 0.71. Most logged clicks happened in the top three slots. In a well-powered two-week A/B test, job applications per search do not change. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The logs reflect the old ranker's choices and slot order, so predicting those clicks better need not mean better rankings.
The held-out week came right after the training weeks, so it shared too much with them, and a week from months later would show no gain.
AUC ignores calibration, and applications depend on well-calibrated click probabilities, so offline log loss would have predicted the flat result.
The offline test scored single impressions while the A/B test split users, and that change of unit alone hides a real gain online.
explanation:
Logged clicks are shaped by the old system. Users mostly click what sits in the top slots, partly because it sits there. That is position bias. And jobs the old ranker never showed have no clicks at all, which is a feedback loop. A new model can get better at predicting these biased clicks, for example by learning what the old ranker liked, without finding jobs that users would apply to. Clicks are also only a proxy for applications, the real goal.

The option about the held-out week has it backwards. A week right after training is the standard choice, and an older week drifts further from current users without removing the bias in the logs. The option about calibration misses that a ranker uses only the order of its scores, and log loss computed on the same biased click logs would share the same blind spot. The option about the unit of analysis is wrong because splitting by user is the normal way to test a ranker. If the new ranker really put better jobs on top, applications per search would rise under a user split too.
deeper: Fixes include position-debiased training (inverse propensity weighting), a small slice of randomised results to collect unbiased labels, and interleaving tests that compare rankers on the same users. A strong candidate also asks whether the offline metric used applications or only clicks.

prompt: An intent classifier for a support bot scores 91% accuracy on a 12,000-ticket test set. Before launch, the team wants to know whether it fails for particular groups, such as users writing in Portuguese or tickets sent from the mobile app. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Report accuracy for each language and channel, side by side with the overall 91%.
Show how many test tickets each slice has, with an interval, so a 40-ticket slice is read with care.
For slices well below 91%, read a sample of their misclassified tickets to find the cause.
Report the plain average of the per-slice accuracies as the overall accuracy, so each group counts once.
Leave out every slice with fewer than 200 test tickets, since such small slices tell you nothing.
Measure each slice on the training set instead, since it has far more tickets per slice than the test set.
explanation:
Slice evaluation exists because a good overall number can hide a group where the model fails. Putting per-slice accuracy next to the overall figure shows which groups lag. Sample size matters because a slice of 40 tickets has a 95% interval of roughly ±12 points around 80% accuracy, so a gap that size may be noise. Reading the errors in a weak slice turns a number into a cause, such as missing training data in one language.

The plain average of slice accuracies is a macro average. It is a useful extra view, but calling it overall accuracy is wrong, since it no longer matches the share of all tickets classified correctly. Dropping small slices hides exactly the groups most likely to be underserved. The better move is to report them with wide intervals and collect more data. Training-set accuracy is inflated by fitting, so it cannot show how the model does on new tickets from any group.
deeper: In practice, slice definitions are agreed before results come in, and new slices found while digging are treated as hypotheses to confirm on fresh data. Interviewers also like hearing that slice metrics belong in monitoring after launch, not only in the pre-launch report.

prompt:
An online grocer measures search rankers by the share of searches that end in an add-to-cart. The new ranker was switched on first for new users, so last month's logs look like this:

- Old ranker: returning users 8,000 searches at 30%, new users 2,000 searches at 10%, overall 26%
- New ranker: returning users 2,000 searches at 32%, new users 8,000 searches at 12%, overall 16%

The new ranker wins in both groups but loses overall. Explain how that happens, and say which comparison should drive the launch decision and how you would get it.
answer: This is Simpson's paradox. The overall rate is a weighted average of the group rates, and the weights differ. New users add to cart far less often whatever the ranker. 80% of the new ranker's searches came from new users, against 20% for the old ranker, so its overall rate is dragged down by its traffic mix, not by worse ranking. Within each group it is 2 points better. Because the mix came from the rollout plan, the within-group comparison is the fair one. I would standardise both rankers to the same mix, such as expected launch traffic, which gives 28% against 26% at an 80/20 mix. The clean answer is a randomised A/B test, where both arms get the same mix. I would also confirm the groups are defined before treatment, because if the ranker changed who counts as a new user, the overall number would matter.
points: Names Simpson's paradox: overall rate is a weighted average with different weights
New users convert less, and the new ranker saw mostly new users
The mix difference comes from the rollout, so compare within groups
Reweight both to a common traffic mix, or run a randomised A/B test
Check the grouping is fixed before treatment and not caused by the ranker
explanation:
The numbers check out. Old ranker: 0.8 × 30% + 0.2 × 10% = 26%. New ranker: 0.2 × 32% + 0.8 × 12% = 16%. The new ranker is better in each group but carries far more of the hard traffic. Reweighting the new ranker to the old mix gives 0.8 × 32% + 0.2 × 12% = 28%, two points above 26%.

The common mistake is to trust the overall number because it uses all the data. All the data is exactly the problem when each ranker saw a different population. The opposite mistake is to always prefer the group view. That is only right when the grouping variable is not changed by the thing being tested. If the new ranker had turned returning users into lapsed ones, the overall drop would be a real effect. Here, who saw which ranker was decided by the rollout plan, so the group view isolates the ranker's effect and the overall view mostly measures the traffic mix.
deeper: Staged rollouts by user type, region or platform create this trap all the time. A strong candidate asks how traffic was assigned before reading any comparison, and prefers a randomised test, or at least a reweighted comparison, over a raw before-and-after number.

prompt: A camera model watches forests for wildfire smoke, and smoke is the positive class. One morning it raises a smoke alert, but the image only shows fog. In the model's confusion matrix, this case is counted as a ______.
explanation:
Read the name in two parts. The second word is what the model predicted: it said smoke, the positive class, so the case is a positive. The first word says whether that prediction was right: there was no smoke, so it was false. Together that makes a false positive. In statistics it is also called a type I error, or in plain words a false alarm.

The common mistake is to answer false negative, reasoning that fog is a negative thing or that the truth was negative. The name follows the prediction, not the truth. A false negative would be the opposite case: real smoke that the model missed. False positives push precision down, because precision divides by everything the model flagged. False negatives push recall down, because recall divides by everything that was really there.
deeper: For a wildfire system the two errors have very different costs. A false positive sends a crew to look at fog, while a false negative lets a fire grow. Interviewers often ask you to name both cells and say which one the business would rather pay for.

prompt: A model summarises customer support calls. For one call, summary X scores ROUGE-L 0.62 against the human reference and summary Y scores 0.41. On reading them, Y is a correct paraphrase of the reference, while X copies much of the reference wording but states the wrong refund amount. What does this show?
options: ROUGE measures word overlap, so it rewards copied wording and treats a wrong amount as one mismatched word.
ROUGE must have been computed wrongly, because a summary with a factual error cannot outscore a correct summary.
Y would come out ahead on BLEU, because BLEU matches synonyms and checks meaning rather than the exact words used.
ROUGE-L fails only on long texts, so scoring single words with ROUGE-1 instead would put Y ahead of X.
explanation:
ROUGE counts how many words or word sequences a summary shares with a reference. ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. Summary X reuses the reference wording, so it overlaps a lot. The wrong refund amount is just one token that does not match, so it costs X about as much as any other changed word. Summary Y says the same facts in new words, so it overlaps less and scores lower even though it is better.

Nothing was computed wrongly. This is ROUGE working as designed, and it has no notion of facts. BLEU has the same blind spot, since it is also built on exact n-gram overlap and does not match synonyms or meaning. Switching to ROUGE-1 does not help either. X still shares more single words with the reference than the paraphrase does, and a wrong number is still only one word.
deeper: Treat BLEU and ROUGE as cheap regression signals, not judges of quality. For summaries, teams add factual checks such as entailment models or an LLM judge with a rubric, plus human review on a sample. Numbers, names and dates deserve targeted checks of their own.

prompt: A card issuer retrains its fraud model every month. Fraud is confirmed by chargebacks, which can arrive up to 60 days after a transaction, and fraudsters change tactics every few weeks. How would you evaluate a new model version before and after it goes live?
answer: Offline, I would split by time, never at random: train on older months and test on a later window, so the test looks like the future the model will face. The test window must end at least 60 days ago, so its labels have matured. Otherwise recent fraud that has not been reported yet is counted as legitimate, which corrupts both precision and recall. I would backtest over several consecutive windows to see how fast performance decays as tactics shift. I would report business metrics at a fixed alert budget, such as fraud dollars caught and the false decline rate, next to PR-AUC. Online, I would run the new model in shadow mode or on a small share of traffic. While labels are pending, I would watch fast signals: score distribution drift, alert rate, analyst review outcomes and early customer disputes. Then I would recompute the real metrics as chargebacks mature.
points: Split by time, training on the past and testing on a later window
Score only on matured labels, at least 60 days old, or fresh fraud looks legitimate
Backtest over several windows to measure decay under drift
Report business metrics at a fixed alert budget, such as dollars caught and false declines
Online, use shadow mode or a small rollout with fast proxy signals until labels arrive
explanation:
Two problems stack up here. Fraud patterns shift, so a random split lets the model see future tactics in training and makes the test look easier than real life. And labels arrive late, so the most recent data is partly mislabelled: a fraudulent transaction from last week usually still looks legitimate in the table.

The most common mistake is to test on the freshest month because it seems most relevant. Its unreported fraud is labelled as legitimate, so a correct alert on it is scored as a false positive and a miss on it is scored as a true negative. The numbers can move in either direction, and they will change again once chargebacks land. Waiting for label maturity costs time, which is why the online plan leans on fast proxies such as analyst review outcomes and score drift. These cannot replace confirmed labels, but they catch a broken model within days instead of two months.
deeper: A strong candidate also mentions that the model's own decisions change the labels. Declined transactions never become chargebacks, so their true label stays unknown. Teams handle this with a small random approval holdout or by labelling declines through analyst review.

prompt: A product manager owns the spam filter for a business email product. They ask you what precision and recall mean for their filter, and which of the two they should keep a closer eye on. How would you explain it?
answer: Precision answers: of the emails we moved to spam, how many really were spam? If precision is 98%, then 2 in every 100 emails in the spam folder were real mail that the customer may never see. Recall answers: of all the spam that arrived, how much did we catch? At 90% recall, 1 in 10 spam emails still reaches the inbox. The two trade off through the score threshold. A stricter filter catches more spam but hides more real mail. For business email I would watch precision first, because a hidden invoice or contract costs far more than one extra spam message a user can delete. In practice I would set a floor on precision, or a cap on how much legitimate mail gets filtered, and then push recall as high as possible within that limit.
points: Precision is the share of filtered emails that really were spam
Recall is the share of all spam that the filter caught
They trade off through the threshold
Watch precision first, because hiding real mail costs more than missing spam
Set a precision floor, then maximise recall within it
explanation:
The key to explaining these to a non-specialist is to tie each metric to a mistake the user feels. Low precision means real mail lands in spam. Low recall means spam lands in the inbox. Then the choice between them becomes a question about which mistake costs more, which the product manager can answer better than anyone.

The common mistake is to define the two with formulas only, or to mix them up by saying precision is how much spam we caught. That is recall. The second mistake is to call one metric enough on its own. A filter that sends everything to spam has perfect recall, and a filter that only catches the most obvious spam can have near perfect precision while missing most of it. That is why the advice is a floor on one and maximising the other, not watching precision alone.
deeper: A sharp follow-up: precision depends on how much spam arrives. On a day with a spam flood, precision rises even if the filter hides the same number of real emails. So many teams also track the false positive rate on legitimate mail, which counts hidden real emails directly.

prompt: Which statements about the ROC curve of a binary classifier are true? Select all that apply.
options: The diagonal from (0, 0) to (1, 1) is what random scores produce on average.
Each point on the curve comes from one choice of decision threshold.
Squaring every score, when all scores lie between 0 and 1, leaves the curve unchanged.
The x-axis shows precision and the y-axis shows recall at each threshold.
Raising the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.7 changes the shape of the curve.
explanation:
An ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate as the threshold sweeps from high to low. Each threshold gives one point, so the curve is a picture of every threshold at once. Random scores flag positives and negatives at the same rate, so TPR equals FPR on average, which is the diagonal. The curve only depends on how the scores order the examples. Squaring numbers between 0 and 1 keeps their order, so every threshold has a matching one that flags exactly the same examples, and the curve does not move.

The statement about precision and recall describes a different plot, the precision-recall curve. The ROC x-axis is the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN). The statement about raising the threshold confuses the curve with a single point on it. Changing the threshold moves you to another point on the same curve. It does not reshape the curve.
deeper: Because ROC depends only on ordering, calibration problems never show up in it. A common follow-up is to ask why a model with a fine ROC curve can still give useless probabilities, and how you would check for that with a reliability diagram.

prompt: An insurer built a claims-fraud model in a market where 5% of claims are fraudulent. There, at the chosen threshold, it has a true positive rate of 0.80 and a false positive rate of 0.04. The same model and threshold are now used in a new market where only 1% of claims are fraudulent. Assume the true positive rate and false positive rate stay the same. What precision should the team expect in the new market? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
check:
tpr = 0.80
fpr = 0.04
prev = 0.01
tp = tpr * prev
fp = fpr * (1 - prev)
result = tp / (tp + fp)
explanation:
Work per 10,000 claims in the new market. 1% are fraud, so 100 fraudulent and 9,900 honest claims.

Step 1, true positives: 0.80 × 100 = 80.

Step 2, false positives: 0.04 × 9,900 = 396.

Step 3, precision = 80 / (80 + 396) = 80 / 476 ≈ 0.168, which is 0.17.

In the original market the same model had 400 true positives and 0.04 × 9,500 = 380 false positives per 10,000, a precision of about 0.51. The model did not get worse at telling fraud from honest claims. TPR and FPR are each measured within one class, so they ignore how common fraud is. Precision mixes the two classes, so when honest claims become a bigger share, the same 4% false alarm rate produces far more false alerts per real hit.

The common mistake is to assume precision carries over at about 0.51 because the model is unchanged. Another is to multiply 0.80 by 0.01 and stop there, which is the true positive share of all claims, not precision.
deeper: This is why investigation teams in a new market can get swamped even when the model is fine. A strong candidate suggests raising the threshold for the new market to bring the alert volume back in line with team capacity, and checking whether TPR and FPR really held, since the fraud patterns may differ too.

prompt: A music streaming app plans an even 50/50 split for an A/B test of a new playlist screen. After a week, control has 503,912 users and treatment has 496,088. A chi-square test comparing these counts with the planned split gives p < 0.0001. Before reading any business metric, the team flags this problem, which usually points to a bug in assignment or logging. The problem is called a ______.
explanation:
A sample ratio mismatch means the users who ended up in each arm do not match the split you planned, by more than chance allows. With 1,000,000 users and a fair 50/50 coin, the count in one arm has a standard deviation of √(1,000,000 × 0.5 × 0.5) = 500. Control is 3,912 above 500,000, nearly 8 standard deviations, and the chi-square value is about 61. That is not luck.

The common mistake is to wave the gap away because 50.4% against 49.6% looks close to even. At large sample sizes even small percentage gaps are far outside chance. The other mistake is to call it selection bias or Simpson's paradox. Those are broader ideas. SRM is the specific check on counts per arm, and when it fails, the users that are missing from one arm are usually not missing at random, for example users whose app crashed before the treatment screen logged them. That biases every metric, so the result should not be trusted until the cause is found.
deeper: Mature experiment platforms run the SRM check automatically and block results when it fails. Common causes include bot filtering that hits one arm more, redirects that drop users, and a treatment that crashes for some devices before the exposure event fires.

subtopic: launch criteria for a ranking model
prompt: A hotel booking site has a new search ranker. Offline, NDCG@10 on human-labelled queries rose from 0.61 to 0.64. A two-week A/B test shows bookings per search up 0.4% (95% confidence interval 0.1% to 0.7%), p95 page latency up 40 ms and the cancellation rate unchanged. What offline metrics, online success metrics and guardrail metrics should be set before such a test, and would you ship this result?
answer: Before the test I would fix three sets. Offline: NDCG@10 on labelled queries, a booking-based metric replayed on logs, and serving latency, used as a gate to decide whether an online test is worth running. Online success: one primary metric agreed in advance, here bookings or revenue per search, with the test length and minimum lift set from a power analysis. Guardrails with limits: page latency, cancellation rate, error rate, revenue per booking and partner coverage. On this result I would lean toward shipping. The interval excludes zero, and 0.4% of bookings is a lot of money at scale. The latency rise is already priced into the measured booking lift, so the question is whether 40 ms stays inside the latency limit set beforehand. I would also check sample ratio, a flat daily lift with no novelty fade, and consistent segments, then ship with a small holdback to confirm the effect lasts.
points: Offline metrics such as NDCG@10 act as a gate, not the launch decision
One primary online metric, such as bookings per search, fixed before the test with a power analysis
Guardrails with preset limits: latency, cancellations, errors, revenue per booking
Ship when the interval excludes zero and every guardrail is inside its limit
Check sample ratio, novelty fade and segments, and keep a holdback after launch
explanation:
Offline NDCG tells you the new ranker orders labelled results better, but labels from raters are not bookings. That is why it works as a gate for spending test traffic, while the launch decision rests on the online primary metric. Guardrails exist because a ranker can raise bookings while hurting something else, such as pushing hotels that get cancelled more, or slowing the page.

The most common mistake is to dismiss a 0.4% lift as too small. Small relative lifts on a core metric at a big booking site are often worth millions a year, and the interval says the lift is real. The opposite mistake is to ship on the lift without checking the guardrails, or to judge the 40 ms after the fact. The limit should be agreed before the test so the decision is not argued from the result. Two weeks also leaves room for a novelty effect, which is why a holdback after launch is worth keeping.
deeper: Interviewers like to push on the latency trade. A strong answer notes that the measured booking lift already includes the latency cost for this test, but that latency adds up across launches, so many teams keep a latency budget and ask a ranker to pay for its milliseconds with a clear lift.
